title: The Communist Manifesto
author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
length: Preamble and four main sections · 213 paragraphs
openingText: A spectre is haunting Europe—the spectre of communism. All the powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise this spectre: Pope and Czar, Metternich and Guizot, French radicals and German police-spies.
about:
The Communist Manifesto is a political pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, published in 1848. It explains historical change through class struggle and argues that the modern bourgeoisie has both transformed the world and created its own opponent: the proletariat. The authors describe the bourgeoisie's revolutionary role before arguing that the working class must acquire political power.

The four main sections examine bourgeois and proletarian society, communist aims, competing socialist tendencies, and relations with contemporary opposition parties. The ten-point programme appears in Section II and is proposed for the most advanced countries. It includes interventions in property rights, progressive income taxation, state centralisation, and free public education. The final section concerns political alliances and ends with an appeal for international unity.

The pamphlet advocates revolution, including the forcible overthrow of the existing social order. It also makes broad historical claims and predictions. Read these as arguments to examine: what examples support them, what conditions do the authors specify, and what actually follows from their analysis? This reading text contains the manifesto itself; later prefaces and a complete historical apparatus of notes are not included.

angleCards.title: The bourgeoisie's double role
angleCards.text: The authors describe the bourgeoisie as a revolutionary force that creates the world market and transforms production. They also claim that it creates the conditions of its own downfall. Follow the connection between these claims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the steps from the bourgeoisie's historical achievements to the prediction of its downfall.

angleCards.title: What does property mean?
angleCards.text: Section II distinguishes personal appropriation for subsistence from property that gives power over others' labour. Read that distinction alongside the concrete proposals about land, inheritance, and credit.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the different meanings of property and how they connect to the programme.

angleCards.title: From analysis to programme
angleCards.text: The ten proposals appear in Section II and are tied to particular historical conditions. They include both social reforms and coercive interventions. Examine their justifications and the results the authors expect.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the relationship between historical analysis, the acquisition of political power, and the ten-point programme.

angleCards.title: Alliances and disagreement
angleCards.text: Section III attacks other socialist tendencies; Section IV describes conditional alliances with other parties. What can these groups work together on, and which disagreements are to be maintained?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the criticism of other socialists with the political alliances in the final section.

cast.name: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
cast.description: The two authors present a joint political argument. They speak on behalf of communists, distinguish their aims from those of other socialist tendencies, and address both workers and opponents.

cast.name: The bourgeoisie
cast.description: The class associated with capital, large-scale industry, and control of the means of production. It appears both as an agent of historical change and as the proletariat's opponent.

cast.name: The proletariat
cast.description: Workers who must sell their labour to live. The authors argue that their struggle can move from scattered resistance toward organisation as a class and the acquisition of political power.

cast.name: The petty bourgeoisie
cast.description: Small manufacturers, merchants, artisans, and peasants appear as groups whose position is threatened by large-scale industry. The text distinguishes their present interests from their possible future as proletarians.

cast.name: Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Owen
cast.description: Section III acknowledges critical insights in their systems but attacks attempts to transform society through invented plans and small experiments. It also distinguishes the founders from their followers.

cast.name: Other opposition parties
cast.description: The final section describes cooperation with Chartists, agrarian reformers, radicals, and others. According to the text, cooperation should not erase the communists' own aims or criticism.

whyItMatters.title: An explanation to test
whyItMatters.body: Class struggle supplies the text's recurring explanation of historical change. Readers can ask whether the examples support it and whether the move from a tendency to an asserted inevitability is justified.

whyItMatters.title: Economics becomes politics
whyItMatters.body: The manifesto connects production, property, labour, and the world market to political power. This lets readers follow each step and ask which conclusions need further support.

whyItMatters.title: Several modes of argument
whyItMatters.body: Rhetorical questions, imagined objections, satire, and concrete demands alternate throughout the pamphlet. Distinguishing analysis, polemic, and programme helps clarify what the text is doing.
